```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pls)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width=5)
```

# Introduction

This vignette contains examples of the functionality that was introduced with version 3.0.0 of the **pls** package. A compact PLSR model will be the basis for all examples. Three groups of functions will be showcased:
- ggplot and Plotly graphics
- tidyverse functions
- wrappers for piping of the base PLSR and PCR function

# Fit a compact model

To demonstrate the ggplot-/Plotly-based plotting capabilities and the tidyverse functions, we start by fitting a simple PLSR model.

```{r fit-model-gg}
data(yarn)
d <- yarn[1:20, , drop = FALSE]
mod <- plsr(density ~ NIR, ncomp = 2, data = d, validation = "CV")
```

# ggplot workflow

If **ggplot2** is installed, the model can be plotted through
`autoplot()` or the dedicated ggplot helpers. If **plotly** is also installed,
interactive plots can be enabled by setting `plotly=TRUE`. Below, we start with the
individual plots, then indicate what the corresponding autoplot() code
would look like, before we end with dashboard plots; static and interactive.

## Score and loading plots

These are the basic plots for viewing the observations and variables through
subspace windows. While score plots are always in the form of scatter plots,
scatter can be turned on and off for loading plots depending on what type
of data are analysed.

```{r ggplot-score-loadings, eval=TRUE}
gg_scoreplot(mod)
gg_loadingplot(mod, scatter = TRUE)
gg_loadingplot(mod)
```

## Interactive selection and refit

If **ggiraph** and **shiny** are installed, selected sample IDs can be returned
from `gg_scoreplot(select = TRUE)` and used with `refit()`. This makes for an
intuitive, visual selection and refit procedure.

```{r optional-interactive, eval=FALSE}
ids <- gg_scoreplot(mod, select = TRUE)
mod_drop <- refit(mod, selection = ids, exclude = TRUE)
mod_keep <- refit(mod, selection = ids, exclude = FALSE)
```

## Biplot and correlation plot

Scores and loadings can also be overlayed in joint scatter
plots called biplots. One can also show how much the variables are correlated
to the scores through correlation plots.

```{r ggplot-bi-corr, eval=TRUE}
gg_biplot(mod)
gg_corrplot(mod)
```

## Prediction plot

Plots of predicted values vs measured values are obtained through
prediction plots.

```{r ggplot-pred, eval=TRUE}
gg_predplot(mod, ncomp = 1:2)
```

## Coefficient plot

Regression coefficients can be visualised through coefficient plots.

```{r ggplot-coef, eval=TRUE}
gg_coefplot(mod, ncomp = 1:2)
```

## Validation plot

Validation metrics can be shown using validation plots.

```{r ggplot-val, eval=TRUE}
gg_valplot(mod, val.type = "R2", estimate = c("train", "CV"))
```

## Raw data plot

Finally, raw data can be visualised through raw data plots. For spectral
data, line plots are most useful, while boxplots and violin plots are
useful for tabular data.

```{r ggplot-raw, eval=TRUE}
gg_rawdataplot(mod, plottype = "line")
```

## autplot()

All the plots above can also be produced using the autoplot() function
associated with ggplot2. 

```{r optional-autoplot, eval=FALSE}
autoplot(mod, type = "scores")
autoplot(mod, type = "loadings")
autoplot(mod, type = "biplot")
autoplot(mod, type = "correlation")
autoplot(mod, type = "prediction")
autoplot(mod, type = "coefficients")
autoplot(mod, type = "validation", val.type = "R2", estimate = c("train", "CV"))
autoplot(mod, type = "rawdata", plottype = "line")
```

## Dashboards

The dashboard plots combine a set of plots to give an overview of the main
aspects of the model. The default is to show scores, loadings, prediction 
and validation metrics as a ggplot2 or Plotly panel. When Plotly is used,
the plot samples and variables are linked such that selection in one panel
affects the selection in all relevant panels.

```{r ggplot-dashboard, eval=TRUE}
# Static dashboard (draws in interactive sessions, returns a gtable invisibly)
gg_dashboard(
  mod,
  panel_args = list(prediction = list(ncomp = 2))
)

# HTML dashboard with Plotly panels
# Object selection is turned on by default.
gg_dashboard(
  mod,
  plotly = TRUE,
  panel_args = list(prediction = list(ncomp = 2))
)
```

# Tidyverse workflow

A compact, tidy-style workflow for `mvr` models is also supported by
the **pls** package, using the methods:

- `tidy()` for long-format model components and validation outputs.
- `glance()` for one-row model summaries.
- `augment()` for sample-wise fitted values and residuals.

## Tidy model components

A long-format table can be generated, containing weights, loadings and
coefficients, or a subset of these.

```{r tidy-components}
comp_tbl <- tidy(mod, what = c("weights", "loadings", "coefficients"))
head(comp_tbl)
```

## Tidy validation metrics

The same type of long-format table can also be used on validation metrics.

```{r tidy-validation}
rmsep_tbl <- tidy(RMSEP(mod, estimate = c("train", "CV")))
head(rmsep_tbl)
```

## One-row summary with glance

Important parameters and metrics can be shown as a one-liner using glance().

```{r glance-summary}
glance(mod)
```

## Sample-wise outputs with augment

Fitted values and residuals (not for new data) can be added to the data
object using the augment() method.

```{r augment-train}
# Add fitted values and residuals for the training data.
aug_train <- augment(mod)
aug_train[1:5, -2]
```

```{r augment-newdata}
# Add fitted values for new data.
aug_new <- augment(mod, data = d[1:5, , drop = FALSE])
aug_new[, -1]
```
